rv.q: A decent vehicle for two superb actors, “The Collaboration” is not some gorgeously poetic drama, nor does it offer new revelation for the ages, nor a feast of formative risk-taking.

It's hard to call this gushing fountain of clever talk a play. There's no dramatic shape to it: No plot, no event, no conflict, no danger. But there are two richly drawn characters on stage with plenty to say for themselves.

Mr. Pope is mesmerizingly good as Basquiat, flooding the stage with the intensity of a man who feels himself assailed by the vampiric tendencies of the art world, and who has been battling other demons all his life.
Like most contemporary art, 'The Collaboration' is attractive and fun to look at, but only as profound as you interpret it to be.
The play imagines what they might have been like behind the masks they fashioned for the public, but rarely gets far beyond the surface.

Onstage, though, “The Collaboration” feels emptily formulaic — less like an insider’s view of its famous subjects’ lives than a kind of biographical tourism that gets into serious gawking in its second half.
This is the kind of static bio-play that brings two famous figures to the stage and then stalls out.
The Collaboration is an oddly lifeless endeavor, a failure in capturing even a moment of simple artistic inspiration much less the ignition of collaborative genius.
That's probably the high point of this otherwise dreary affair.
Pope gives a truly moving performance as the flirtatious and ephemeral Basquiat.
The show suffers from forgettable writing, but there are a few vibrant moments, thanks entirely to the lead performances that are a marvel (no Bettany/Vision pun intended) to witness.
McCarten’s play is not entirely convincing although it is certainly effective as an entertainment.

These are the sort of questions that arise here and there during “The Collaboration,” which has a script that can feel surprisingly clunky, in both moments of exposition and in the overall plot, which is largely predictable, even as the actors somehow redeem it.

But the story unfolds with so little urgency or new information that it feels not unlike passing through a museum gift shop: Here are a few anecdotes and trinkets to take home, something comfortably concrete on which to hang the vast unknowability of modern art.

The urgency of the second act, and the energetic peaks in the men’s performances—particularly Pope’s—give The Collaboration some much-needed electricity, but the stilted staging of the play leaks power and focus from a show which determinedly keeps its protagonists a mystery.
But for all the actors’ enthusiastic histrionics, the script rarely seems more than a series of contrivances more artfully artificial than artistically authentic.
Though the writing is a letdown, The Collaboration nonetheless proves entertaining, thanks to the colorful figures at its center and the superb acting.
The same could also be said of The Collaboration, which relies on an intense curiosity about two of the most recognizable names in modern art.
The Collaboration goes in one ear and out the other, not quite befitting of the legacy of the two artists at its center.
The real problem is that Beane has written a play that's more interested in being clever than in being honest, and more interested in being topical than in being timeless.
It’s the only way you’ll leave the theater satisfied.

If only the Tonys gave out such an award, Dick and Robinson would deserve it, because just about the only thing that Anthony McCarten’s new play gets right are the wigs worn by the characters he has named Andy Warhol and Jean-Michel Basquiat.

Each character is as thin as a Campbell’s soup label, but the insistence to ask these rote questions, then cop out of answering any when they turn to why the street artist himself is so comfortable with his funds is frustrating.
That famous collaboration is at the center of Anthony McCarten’s new play which remains surfacely cerebral rather than thought-provoking.
But as Broadway proves time and again, commercial and artistic success are not mutually exclusive.
Pope and Bethany look the parts but the script isn't compelling enough.
As for Pope, you can’t take your eyes off his Basquiat– a dynamo who literally leaps around the stage, exploding with creativity.
All of this plays a bit with historical facts, seeing as in actuality, Basquiat was thrilled to work with Warhol and craved his benediction.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on this bioplay about Warhol and Basquiat, praising Bettany and Pope's performances but finding McCarten's script surface-level and talky, with many calling it a competent but shallow exploration of the artists' collaboration.

vs.sum: The Samuel J. Friedman Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and a well-raked mezzanine, ensuring a clear view from most seats. The sound quality is consistently praised, and the seating is comfortable with decent legroom. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant design following renovation, though facilities like restrooms are average, leading to some congestion during intermissions.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Built-in induction loop for t-coil hearing aids.
